helpGuides.subtitle: Learn how to make the most of ShipFlow with our comprehensive guides
helpGuides.welcomeDesc: ShipFlow helps teams implement the Shape Up methodology for product development. These guides will help you understand and effectively use all features of the platform.

helpGuides.cooldownActivitiesDesc: Manage bug fixes, tech debt, research, and other work during cooldown periods.

helpGuides.interactiveTourDesc: Click the help icon in the header to start an interactive tour of the application.
helpGuides.aiAssistantDesc: Use the floating Q&A button on any page to ask questions about your cycles and projects.

helpGuides.publicApiDesc: Access ShipFlow programmatically via our REST API and OpenAPI specification.
helpGuides.ideaToRoadmapDesc: Follow the full journey of an idea — from raw concept to shaped pitch, betting, and roadmap visibility.
helpGuides.mcpServerDesc: Learn how Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers supercharge ShipFlow AI with external context.
helpGuides.importDataDesc: Bring your existing work from Jira, Linear, or Asana using CSV upload or direct API import.

gettingStarted.intro: ShipFlow is a project management tool built around the Shape Up methodology developed by Basecamp. It helps teams work in focused cycles, make informed betting decisions, and track progress through hill charts.
gettingStarted.shapeUpDesc: Shape Up is a product development methodology that emphasizes fixed time, variable scope, and small batch sizes. Teams work in 6-week cycles with 2-week cool-down periods.

gettingStarted.step1Item3: Click "Sign In" to access your workspace

aiRiskAdvisor.title: Using AI Risk Advisor
aiRiskAdvisor.subtitle: Leverage AI-powered insights to identify risks and improve your planning
aiRiskAdvisor.whatTitle: What is the AI Risk Advisor?
aiRiskAdvisor.whatDesc: The **AI Risk Advisor** is an intelligent assistant that analyzes your pitches, cycles, and projects to identify potential risks, dependencies, and areas of concern before they become problems.
aiRiskAdvisor.howWorksDesc: The AI analyzes your pitch descriptions, scope items, historical data, and team capacity to provide contextual risk assessments and recommendations.
aiRiskAdvisor.whereTitle: Where to Find AI Risk Assessments
aiRiskAdvisor.pitchDetailDesc: View AI-generated risk assessments for individual pitches, including scope risks, technical complexity, and dependency warnings.
aiRiskAdvisor.cycleOverviewDesc: See aggregate risk scores and health metrics for entire cycles, helping you understand overall cycle health.
aiRiskAdvisor.bettingTableDesc: Risk indicators appear next to each pitch during betting meetings, helping inform your commitment decisions.
aiRiskAdvisor.qaPanelDesc: Ask the AI specific questions about risks, dependencies, or concerns using the floating Q&A button.
aiRiskAdvisor.screenshotAlt: AI Risk Advisor panel showing risk assessment and recommendations
aiRiskAdvisor.scoresIntro: The AI assigns risk scores on a scale, typically categorized as:
aiRiskAdvisor.lowRiskDesc: Well-defined scope, clear approach, no major dependencies. Proceed with confidence.
aiRiskAdvisor.mediumRiskDesc: Some uncertainties or dependencies identified. Review recommendations and consider mitigation strategies.
aiRiskAdvisor.highRiskDesc: Significant concerns about scope, complexity, or feasibility. May need reshaping or descoping.
aiRiskAdvisor.scopeRiskDesc: Vague or overly broad deliverables that lack clear boundaries.
aiRiskAdvisor.complexityRiskDesc: Technical challenges, unfamiliar technology, or architectural unknowns.
aiRiskAdvisor.dependencyRiskDesc: Reliance on external teams, APIs, or incomplete work from other pitches.
aiRiskAdvisor.capacityRiskDesc: Team overload, insufficient skillset, or timeline constraints.
aiRiskAdvisor.recommendation1: Read the full AI assessment to understand context
aiRiskAdvisor.recommendation2: Discuss flagged risks during pitch shaping or betting meetings
aiRiskAdvisor.recommendation3: Update pitch scope or appetites based on recommendations
aiRiskAdvisor.recommendation4: Mark risks as "acknowledged" or "mitigated" to track progress
aiRiskAdvisor.aiFindsItem1: Lack of specific metrics or success criteria
aiRiskAdvisor.aiFindsItem2: No mention of which parts of the dashboard
aiRiskAdvisor.aiFindsItem3: No appetite or scope boundaries defined
aiRiskAdvisor.aiSuggestsItem3: Break into Small Batch (1 week) vs Big Batch (6 weeks)
aiRiskAdvisor.qaDesc: Click the floating **Q&A** button (bottom right) to ask the AI specific questions about your work:
aiRiskAdvisor.qaExample1: "What are the biggest risks for Cycle 3?"
aiRiskAdvisor.qaExample3: "How risky is combining these two scopes?"
aiRiskAdvisor.qaNote: The AI will respond based on your project data and Shape Up best practices.
aiRiskAdvisor.feedbackDesc: Help improve AI accuracy by voting on recommendations:
aiRiskAdvisor.feedbackImpact: Your feedback trains the model for better future assessments.
aiRiskAdvisor.limitsSubtitle: What AI can and cannot do
aiRiskAdvisor.limitItem1: **AI is advisory:** It highlights potential issues but doesn't replace human judgment.
aiRiskAdvisor.limitItem2: **Garbage in, garbage out:** AI quality depends on clear, detailed pitch descriptions.
aiRiskAdvisor.limitItem3: **Update pitches:** If you reshape a pitch, re-run the AI analysis to get updated insights.
aiRiskAdvisor.limitItem4: **Not a blocker:** Risk flags are warnings, not hard stops. Teams can still bet on high-risk pitches if they accept the tradeoffs.

bettingMeeting.subtitle: Learn how to conduct effective betting meetings and make informed cycle commitments
bettingMeeting.whatDesc: A **betting meeting** is where stakeholders decide which pitches to commit to for the next cycle. It's called "betting" because you're placing bets on what will deliver the most value given the fixed time constraint.
bettingMeeting.keyPrincipleDesc: In Shape Up, you bet on pitches, not tasks. Each pitch should be well-shaped with clear boundaries and appetite (time budget).

bettingMeeting.step1Desc: Navigate to the **Pitch Board** to see all available pitches for consideration.
bettingMeeting.step2Desc: Click on each pitch to review its details. Look for:
bettingMeeting.step3Desc: Use the AI Risk Advisor to identify potential issues before committing. This can reveal hidden complexities or dependencies.

hillCharts.title: Understanding Hill Charts
hillCharts.subtitle: Master the hill chart visualization to track progress and identify risks
hillCharts.whatDesc: A **hill chart** is a unique visualization tool from the Shape Up methodology that shows where work items are in their journey from unknown to known to done.
hillCharts.unlike: Unlike traditional progress bars or burn-down charts, hill charts reveal the *nature* of the work being done, not just the quantity completed.
hillCharts.keyInsightDesc: A task stuck on the uphill side indicates uncertainty and unknowns, while movement downhill shows confident execution.
hillCharts.readingTitle: How to Read a Hill Chart
hillCharts.position1Desc: Work just started, lots of unknowns, team is exploring and researching
hillCharts.position2Desc: Making progress on figuring things out, but still facing uncertainties
hillCharts.position3Desc: Critical transition point - unknowns are resolved, ready to execute
hillCharts.position4Desc: Confident execution, clear path to completion, predictable timeline
hillCharts.position5Desc: Work is complete and ready for delivery
hillCharts.movingStep1: Navigate to a pitch or cycle hill chart
hillCharts.movingStep2: Click and drag any item (scope or task) on the chart
hillCharts.movingStep3: Position it based on your current understanding:
hillCharts.movingStep3a: Left side if you're still figuring things out
hillCharts.movingStep3b: Right side if you know what to do and are executing
hillCharts.warnStuckUphill: **Stuck uphill:** Item hasn't moved in days - may need help or discussion
hillCharts.warnMovingBackward: **Moving backward:** New unknowns discovered - reassess scope or approach
hillCharts.warnTooManyUphill: **Too many uphill:** Cycle may be overloaded with uncertain work

circuitBreaker.title: Circuit Breaker
circuitBreaker.subtitle: The Shape Up safety valve - detect and respond to scope overflow
circuitBreaker.principleTitle: The Fixed Time, Variable Scope Principle
circuitBreaker.principleDesc: In Shape Up methodology, **time is fixed**, not scope. When a pitch consistently goes over its appetite (time budget), it signals a fundamental problem: the scope wasn't properly shaped or unexpected complexity emerged.
circuitBreaker.wisdomDesc: "If a pitch is taking too long, something is wrong. You don't extend the deadline—you either cut scope or kill the pitch."
circuitBreaker.mechanismDesc: The Circuit Breaker is ShipFlow's automated mechanism to flag these situations and help teams make the tough decisions that Shape Up requires.
circuitBreaker.step1Desc: ShipFlow tracks work logs against each pitch's appetite (time budget) in real-time.
circuitBreaker.step2Desc: When a pitch reaches your configured threshold (default 80% of appetite), it appears in the overflow detection list with color-coded severity.
circuitBreaker.step3Desc: When you trigger a circuit breaker, all team members assigned to the pitch receive a dashboard notification to discuss the situation.
circuitBreaker.accessSubtitle: Where to find and configure overflow detection
circuitBreaker.accessStep2: Click the **Circuit Breaker** button (⚡ icon) in the header
circuitBreaker.accessStep3: Adjust the threshold slider to detect pitches at different budget consumption levels
circuitBreaker.accessTipDesc: Adjust the detection threshold slider (50-150%) to match your team's tolerance for scope expansion. Conservative teams use 80%, more flexible teams may use 100%.
circuitBreaker.triggerSubtitle: When to flag a pitch for team discussion
circuitBreaker.triggerDesc: When a pitch appears in the overflow list, you can **trigger the circuit breaker** to:
circuitBreaker.triggerItem1: Alert the team that this pitch needs immediate attention
circuitBreaker.triggerItem2: Document the specific overflow reason (e.g., "Unexpected API complexity")
circuitBreaker.triggerItem3: Force a conversation about scope reduction or pitch cancellation
circuitBreaker.triggerItem4: Generate dashboard notifications for all pitch stakeholders
circuitBreaker.triggerDoes1: ✓ Flags the pitch with a red "Circuit Breaker" badge
circuitBreaker.triggerDoes2: ✓ Sends notifications to all team members
circuitBreaker.triggerDoes3: ✓ Adds 50 risk points in risk analysis
circuitBreaker.triggerDoes4: ✓ Moves pitch to high-priority discussion queue
circuitBreaker.triggerAfter: After triggering, the team should meet to decide: **cut scope** or **kill the pitch**.
circuitBreaker.killSubtitle: The hardest but sometimes necessary decision
circuitBreaker.killDesc: When scope can't be cut enough to finish within the appetite, Shape Up says: **kill it**. This isn't failure—it's discipline.
circuitBreaker.killDoes2: • Notifies all team members with the cancellation reason
circuitBreaker.killDoes3: • Preserves work logs and history for future reference
circuitBreaker.killDoes4: • Frees up team capacity for other work
circuitBreaker.killWhen1: It's consistently running 50%+ over appetite with no end in sight
circuitBreaker.killWhen2: The core problem turned out to be different than shaped
circuitBreaker.killWhen3: Technical complexity emerged that makes the appetite unrealistic
circuitBreaker.killWhen4: The business value no longer justifies the expanded investment
circuitBreaker.killRememberDesc: A killed pitch isn't wasted work. The learnings inform better shaping for future cycles. You can always re-pitch with a better understanding and more realistic appetite.
circuitBreaker.resolveDesc: If the team successfully cuts scope and gets back on track, you can **resolve the circuit breaker**:
circuitBreaker.resolveStep3: The pitch returns to normal tracking without the warning flag
circuitBreaker.repitchSubtitle: Learning from overflow and trying again
circuitBreaker.repitchDesc: A killed pitch isn't a failure—it's valuable learning. You can re-pitch the work for the next betting table with a better understanding of the complexity.
circuitBreaker.repitchHow1: During cooldown, analyze what went wrong: Was scope unclear? Did unknowns emerge?
circuitBreaker.repitchHow2: Break the original pitch into smaller, more focused pitches
circuitBreaker.repitchHow3: Set more realistic appetites based on what you learned
circuitBreaker.repitchHow4: Present the refined pitch(es) at the next betting table
circuitBreaker.repitchEx2Text: Team realizes scope was too broad—avatar upload alone is complex
circuitBreaker.repitchEx3Text: Re-pitch as "Basic Profile Edit" (24h) + "Avatar Upload" (16h) - two focused pitches
circuitBreaker.repitchWisdom: Shape Up wisdom: "The best teams kill pitches early and re-pitch smarter, not harder."

cooldownActivities.title: Cooldown Activities
cooldownActivities.subtitle: Manage work during Shape Up cooldown periods - bug fixes, tech debt, research, and more
cooldownActivities.whatIsDesc1: In Shape Up methodology, after each 6-week Build cycle, teams take a 2-week **Cooldown** period. This isn't vacation time—it's dedicated time for flexible, unstructured work that doesn't fit into shaped pitches.
cooldownActivities.shapeUpQuoteText: "Cooldown is breathing room. It's time to fix bugs, explore new ideas, pay down technical debt, and do the small improvements that keep the product healthy."
cooldownActivities.whatIsDesc2: During cooldown, the team has **no committed pitches**, so they can respond to urgent issues, experiment with new technologies, or tackle smaller improvements without the pressure of a fixed-scope deadline.
cooldownActivities.vsBacklogDesc: This is a common point of confusion. Here's the key difference:
cooldownActivities.backlogPoint1: Created **during a Build cycle** (6-week active development)
cooldownActivities.backlogPoint2: Always linked to a **specific pitch** that was committed at betting
cooldownActivities.backlogPoint3: Contribute to shaped, scoped work with appetite estimates
cooldownActivities.backlogPoint4: Tracked on the **Hill Chart** to show progress through uncertainty
cooldownActivities.cooldownPoint1: Created **during the Cooldown period** (2-week flexible time)
cooldownActivities.cooldownPoint2: **Not linked to any pitch**—standalone flexible work items
cooldownActivities.cooldownPoint3: No shaped scope or appetite—just estimates for planning
cooldownActivities.cooldownPoint4: **Not tracked on Hill Chart**—simple status tracking (Planned, In Progress, Completed, Cancelled)
cooldownActivities.typesDesc: ShipFlow supports 11 types of cooldown work:
cooldownActivities.techDebtDesc: Refactor messy code, upgrade dependencies, improve test coverage, or reduce architectural debt.
cooldownActivities.bugFixDesc: Address bugs that emerged during the cycle or from production. Quick fixes that don't require full pitch shaping.
cooldownActivities.refactoringDesc: Restructure code to improve readability, maintainability, and performance without changing external behavior.
cooldownActivities.kickoffPrepDesc: Prepare for the next cycle: set up environments, configure tools, or create templates for upcoming pitches.
cooldownActivities.learningDesc: Learn new tools, attend workshops, document best practices, or skill up on technologies needed for future work.
cooldownActivities.qaDesc: Write automated tests, perform manual testing, improve test coverage, or validate edge cases.
cooldownActivities.documentationDesc: Write architecture docs, update API documentation, create onboarding guides, or improve README files.
cooldownActivities.infrastructureDesc: Set up CI/CD pipelines, configure monitoring, optimize build processes, or improve deployment automation.
cooldownActivities.researchDesc: Investigate new technologies, explore potential solutions, or spike on uncertain technical approaches.
cooldownActivities.planningDesc: Roadmap planning, backlog grooming, or preparing pitch ideas for upcoming betting tables.
cooldownActivities.otherDesc: Any other valuable cooldown work that doesn't fit into the standard categories.
cooldownActivities.accessStep1: Navigate to your **Cycle Detail** page during a cycle in the COOLDOWN phase
cooldownActivities.accessStep2: Click the **"Cooldown Activities"** button in the cycle header
cooldownActivities.accessStep3: You'll see a dashboard with summary cards (total activities, completion rate, estimated/actual hours) and a list of all cooldown activities with filters
cooldownActivities.practice1: **Keep it Small:** Cooldown activities should be completable in 1-3 days. Larger work needs to be shaped into a pitch.
cooldownActivities.practice2: **Document Outcomes:** For research and experiments, record findings so future cycles can benefit.
cooldownActivities.practice3: **Balance Types:** Don't spend all cooldown on bugs. Mix in tech debt, learning, and exploration.
cooldownActivities.practice4: **Track Actual Hours:** Log time spent so you can see if estimates are realistic and plan future cooldowns better.
cooldownActivities.practice5: **Don't Overcommit:** Cooldown is breathing room. It's okay if you don't finish everything—the important part is giving the team flexibility.

ideaToRoadmap.title: Idea to Roadmap
ideaToRoadmap.subtitle: Follow the full journey of an idea — from raw concept to shaped pitch, betting table, and roadmap visibility
ideaToRoadmap.shapeUpNoticeDesc: This guide covers the pitch lifecycle used in Shape Up projects. Kanban projects use a simpler task-based flow without pitches or betting.
ideaToRoadmap.lifecycleTitle: The Pitch Lifecycle at a Glance
ideaToRoadmap.lifecycleDesc: Every idea follows this journey through ShipFlow before it appears on your roadmap.
ideaToRoadmap.keyConceptDesc: In Shape Up, ideas don't go straight into a backlog. They are shaped into pitches with clear boundaries, then bet on during a betting meeting before any work begins.
ideaToRoadmap.step1Subtitle: Create a new pitch in the IDEA column
ideaToRoadmap.step1Intro: Ideas are the raw starting point. Anyone on the team can capture an idea — it's just a title and a brief description of the problem or opportunity.
ideaToRoadmap.step1Action1: Navigate to the Pitch Board (Cycle Workspace → Pitch Board in the sidebar)
ideaToRoadmap.step1Action2: Click the "+" button in the IDEA column
ideaToRoadmap.step1Action3: Enter a title that describes the problem, not the solution
ideaToRoadmap.step1Action4: Add a short description of what you've observed and why it matters
ideaToRoadmap.step1Tip: Don't worry about solutions yet. The IDEA column is for capturing raw problems and opportunities. You'll shape the solution later.
ideaToRoadmap.step2Subtitle: Flesh out the idea with problem, solution, and boundaries
ideaToRoadmap.step2Intro: When an idea looks promising, move it to DRAFT and start shaping it. A draft adds structure around the raw idea.
ideaToRoadmap.step2Field1Desc: What specific problem does this solve? Who is affected?
ideaToRoadmap.step2Field2Desc: A high-level approach — not a spec, but a direction.
ideaToRoadmap.step2Field3Desc: Known risks or complexities to watch out for.
ideaToRoadmap.step2Field4Desc: What is explicitly out of scope for this pitch.
ideaToRoadmap.step3Subtitle: Set the appetite and confirm the pitch is ready to bet on
ideaToRoadmap.step3Intro: Shaping means the pitch is well-defined enough to present at a betting meeting. Moving to SHAPED requires setting an appetite — the maximum time you're willing to spend.
ideaToRoadmap.step3Check1: The problem is clearly defined and worth solving
ideaToRoadmap.step3Check2: The solution is sketched at the right level of abstraction (not too detailed, not too vague)
ideaToRoadmap.step3Check3: Rabbit holes have been identified and addressed
ideaToRoadmap.step3Check4: An appetite has been set (e.g. 2 weeks, 6 weeks) — this is a time budget, not an estimate
ideaToRoadmap.step3AiDesc: ShipFlow can automatically analyze your pitch for risks using AI. Check the risk score on the pitch detail page to see potential issues before the betting meeting.
ideaToRoadmap.step4Subtitle: The betting meeting decides which shaped pitches get built
ideaToRoadmap.step4Intro: Shaped pitches are presented at the betting meeting. Decision-makers review them and decide which ones to commit to in the upcoming cycle.
ideaToRoadmap.step4Action1: Navigate to the Betting page (Cycle Workspace → Betting in the sidebar)
ideaToRoadmap.step4Action2: Review shaped pitches and discuss with your team
ideaToRoadmap.step4Action3: Accept the pitch into a cycle — this moves it to PENDING status and assigns it to the selected cycle
ideaToRoadmap.step4Tip: Not every shaped pitch gets bet on. It's normal for pitches to wait multiple cycles. Rejected pitches can be reshaped or archived.
ideaToRoadmap.step4LearnMore: Learn more about running effective betting meetings:
ideaToRoadmap.step5Subtitle: Connect your pitch to the roadmap hierarchy
ideaToRoadmap.step5Intro: To make your pitch visible on the roadmap, link it to an epic. Epics group related pitches and belong to initiatives — the top-level strategic goals.
ideaToRoadmap.step5EpicDesc: Group of related pitches within an initiative
ideaToRoadmap.step5PitchDesc: A shaped, time-boxed unit of work
ideaToRoadmap.step5Action1: Open the pitch detail page — in the header, you'll see an epic selector dropdown next to the team and cycle info
ideaToRoadmap.step5Action2: Use the dropdown to pick an existing epic, or go to Planning → Epics first to create one and link it to an initiative
ideaToRoadmap.step5Action3: The pitch now appears on the roadmap timeline under its epic and initiative — you can change or remove the epic any time from the same dropdown
ideaToRoadmap.step6Subtitle: Your idea is now a roadmap item with timeline visibility
ideaToRoadmap.step6Intro: Once a pitch is linked to an epic (and the epic belongs to an initiative), it appears on the interactive roadmap timeline.
ideaToRoadmap.step6Action1: Navigate to Planning → Roadmap in the sidebar
ideaToRoadmap.step6Action2: Expand an initiative to see its epics, then expand an epic to see its pitches
ideaToRoadmap.step6Action3: Use the quarterly/yearly toggle to adjust the timeline view
ideaToRoadmap.step6TimelineDesc: You can drag timeline bars to set or adjust dates for initiatives and epics. Click "Set dates" on items without dates to give them a default two-week window.
ideaToRoadmap.statusRefDesc: Quick reference for all pitch statuses and what they mean
ideaToRoadmap.statusIdeaDesc: Raw concept — just a title and brief description
ideaToRoadmap.statusDraftDesc: Problem and solution are being fleshed out
ideaToRoadmap.statusShapedDesc: Ready for the betting table — appetite is set
ideaToRoadmap.statusPendingDesc: Accepted into a cycle, waiting to start
ideaToRoadmap.statusStartedDesc: Work has begun in the cycle

cycleSetup.title: Setting Up Your First Cycle
cycleSetup.subtitle: Complete walkthrough of creating and managing a work cycle in ShipFlow
cycleSetup.whatDesc: In Shape Up, a **cycle** is a fixed period of time (typically 6 weeks) during which teams work on committed pitches. Cycles provide rhythm and focus, with clear start and end dates.
cycleSetup.keyConceptDesc: After each 6-week cycle, there's a 2-week "cool-down" period for bug fixes, exploration, and planning the next cycle.
cycleSetup.step1Subtitle: Set up the basic cycle structure
cycleSetup.step2Title: Step 2: Adding Pitches to the Cycle
cycleSetup.step2Subtitle: Commit to the work you'll tackle
cycleSetup.importantDesc: Once a cycle starts, avoid changing the end date. Fixed time is a core principle of Shape Up.
cycleSetup.step2Desc: After creating a cycle, add the pitches that were approved during the betting meeting:
cycleSetup.step2Option1Title: Option 1: From the Cycle Detail Page
cycleSetup.step2Option1Step1: Open the cycle you just created
cycleSetup.step2Option1Step2: Look for the **"Add Pitch"** or **"Manage Pitches"** button
cycleSetup.step2Option1Step3: Select pitches from the available list
cycleSetup.step2Option2Step2: For each approved pitch, select the cycle from the dropdown
cycleSetup.step2Option2Step3: The pitch is automatically added to that cycle
cycleSetup.step3Desc: Each pitch in the cycle needs a small team (typically 1-2 people) assigned to it:
cycleSetup.step3Step1: From the cycle detail page, click on a pitch
cycleSetup.step3Step2: In the pitch detail view, look for the **"Assign Team"** section
cycleSetup.step3TipDesc: Keep teams small. Two people working together can move faster and communicate better than larger groups.
cycleSetup.step3AssignCycleTeamTitle: Assign Teams to the Cycle First
cycleSetup.step3AssignCycleTeamDesc: Before generating betting slots, go to the Betting Table and use the Teams for this Cycle panel to assign teams explicitly to the cycle. Teams assigned here — not just to individual pitches — are used for slot generation.
cycleSetup.step4Title: Step 4: Tracking Progress During the Cycle
cycleSetup.step4UseHillDesc: Navigate to the cycle's hill chart to see visual progress of all pitches. Team members should update their positions regularly.
cycleSetup.step4HealthDesc: Visit **Health Overview** to see aggregate metrics:

qaTesting.title: QA & Testing
qaTesting.subtitle: Manage test cases, run manual tests, and track bugs within your cycles
qaTesting.integratedDesc: ShipFlow integrates QA directly into the development cycle. Instead of treating testing as an afterthought, you can define test cases alongside your scopes and track quality in real-time.
qaTesting.testCasesSubtitle: Define how features should be verified
qaTesting.testCasesStep3a: **Title:** Clear, concise summary of what's being tested
qaTesting.testCasesStep3d: **Expected Result:** What should happen if successful
qaTesting.testCasesStep4: Link it to a specific **Pitch** or **Cycle** to track coverage
qaTesting.bestPracticeDesc: Create test cases during the "Shaping" phase or early in the "Build" phase to clarify requirements before code is written.
qaTesting.aiGenerationSubtitle: Speed up test creation with AI
qaTesting.aiGenerationDesc: Speed up test creation with AI-powered generation
qaTesting.aiDesc: ShipFlow can automatically generate test cases based on your pitch descriptions and scope definitions.
qaTesting.aiHowToStep1: Go to **Generate with AI** in the Test Cases page
qaTesting.aiHowToStep2: Select the **Pitch** you want to test
qaTesting.aiHowToStep4: Click **"Save Selected"** to add them to your library
qaTesting.aiWhyItem1: Discover edge cases you might miss
qaTesting.aiWhyItem2: Save time on writing boilerplate steps
qaTesting.bugReportsDesc: When a test fails or you find an issue during exploratory testing, log a bug report.

exportData.title: Export Data
exportData.subtitle: Learn how to export cycle summaries and extract your data from ShipFlow.
exportData.cycleSummaryBody: ShipFlow automatically generates cycle narratives that summarize everything your team accomplished during a 6-week cycle. You can export these as clean Markdown files to share in company wikis, emails, or update posts.
exportData.cycleSummaryStep1: Navigate to the **Dashboard** or a specific **Cycle** view.
exportData.cycleSummaryStep3: Click the **Download** icon (or Export to Markdown) at the top right of the narrative.
exportData.cycleSummaryStep4: A `.md` file will be generated immediately containing the structured summary.
exportData.portabilityBody: All your data in ShipFlow belongs to you. To extract raw data for backup or migration purposes:
exportData.portabilityItem1: **Public REST API:** Use the REST API to bulk export pitches, cycles, and tasks in JSON format.
exportData.portabilityItem2: **Database Access:** If you are self-hosting, you have direct access to the PostgreSQL database for complete pg_dump backups.
exportData.portabilityNote: Built-in CSV export for tables is planned for a future release to make raw data extraction even easier.

mcpServer.title: MCP Server Setup
mcpServer.subtitle: Learn how Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers supercharge ShipFlow AI with external context.
mcpServer.whatBody: The **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** allows ShipFlow's internal AI (like Wise Architecture and Risk Advisor) to securely access your external tools and data sources. By setting up MCP servers, ShipFlow can read your code repositories and design files directly, resulting in vastly superior AI recommendations that are grounded in your actual project reality.
mcpServer.githubBody: With the GitHub MCP, Wise Architecture can read your `package.json`, `pom.xml`, branch structures, and actual code files to suggest libraries and architecture patterns that fit your existing tech stack.
mcpServer.githubStep2: Provide your GitHub App credentials or Personal Access Token.
mcpServer.githubStep3: Ensure the environment variable `MCP_GITHUB_ENABLED=true` is set on your ShipFlow backend server.
mcpServer.figmaBody: The Figma MCP integration allows ShipFlow to pull node and frame data from linked Figma URLs inside pitches. The AI reads this design context to better estimate frontend complexity and required components.
mcpServer.figmaStep1: Navigate to **Organization Settings** > **Integrations** > **MCP Integration** (or Figma settings).
mcpServer.figmaStep2: Store your organization's Figma Access Token.
mcpServer.figmaStep3: Ensure `MCP_FIGMA_ENABLED=true` and `MCP_FIGMA_SERVER_URL` point to your running Figma MCP server instance.

import.title: Import Data
import.subtitle: Bring your existing work from Jira, Linear, or Asana into ShipFlow using CSV upload or direct API import.
import.overviewDesc: Choose the import method that fits your situation
import.overviewBody: ShipFlow supports two ways to bring data from other tools. Use CSV import when you want a one-time bulk migration using a file export. Use API import (Linear or Jira) when you want a direct, OAuth-authenticated connection that pulls data without intermediate files.
import.csvOptionDesc: Export a CSV from your current tool and upload it. Good for Asana or when OAuth setup is not feasible. One-time migration.
import.apiOptionDesc: Connect via OAuth2 and pull data directly. No CSV file needed. Supports Linear and Jira Cloud.
import.overviewNote: In all cases, imported data lands in a Kanban project.
import.overviewNoteDesc: You can switch to Scrum or Shape Up mode at any time from Project Settings after the import is complete.
import.csvDesc: Export a CSV from your current tool, then upload it to ShipFlow
import.jiraExportStep1: Open your Jira project and go to **Project settings**.
import.jiraExportStep3: Select **Export Excel CSV (all fields)** or **Export Excel CSV (current fields)**.
import.jiraExportStep4: Save the `.csv` file to your computer.
import.linearExportStep1: In Linear, go to **Settings** (⚙ icon in the sidebar).
import.linearExportStep2: Click **Export data** under the Workspace section.
import.linearExportStep3: Choose **Issues CSV** and download the file.
import.asanaExportStep1: Open the project you want to export in Asana.
import.asanaExportStep2: Click the **three-dot menu** at the top right of the project.
import.asanaExportStep3: Select **Export / Print** → **CSV**. Asana will email you the file.
import.uploadStep1Desc: Navigate to Import in the sidebar. Drag-and-drop or select your CSV file. ShipFlow auto-detects the source format (Jira, Linear, Asana, or Generic) from column headers.
import.uploadStep2Desc: Review the parsed rows, field mapping, and any validation warnings before committing. Rows with errors are highlighted.
import.uploadStep3Desc: Click Import to process the file. A summary shows imported rows, failed rows, and a link to the new project.
import.fieldMappingNote: Custom fields and file attachments are not imported. Sub-tasks are imported as top-level tasks.
import.linearApiDesc: Connect ShipFlow directly to Linear via OAuth2 — no CSV file required
import.linearApiBody: The Linear API import uses OAuth2 to authenticate your Linear workspace and GraphQL to fetch issues, cycles, and projects in real time.
import.linearApiStep1: Go to **Import** in the ShipFlow sidebar and click the **Linear** tab.
import.linearApiStep2: Click **Connect Linear** and complete the OAuth2 authorization flow in the popup.
import.linearApiStep3: Select the Linear team you want to import from the dropdown.
import.linearApiStep4: Enter a name for the new ShipFlow project and click **Import from Linear**.
import.linearApiWhat1: Issues → Tasks (with priority, status, and assignee)
import.linearApiWhat2: Cycles → Cycles (with start date and end date)
import.jiraApiDesc: Connect ShipFlow to Jira Cloud via Atlassian OAuth 2.0 (3-legged) — no CSV file required
import.jiraApiBody: The Jira API import uses Atlassian's OAuth 2.0 three-legged flow to authenticate your Atlassian account and REST API to fetch issues, sprints, and epics.
import.jiraApiStep1: Go to **Import** in the ShipFlow sidebar and click the **Jira** tab.
import.jiraApiStep2: Click **Connect Jira** and authorize ShipFlow in the Atlassian OAuth popup.
import.jiraApiStep3: Select the Jira project from the dropdown (your cloud workspace is auto-detected).
import.jiraApiStep4: Enter a name for the new ShipFlow project and click **Import from Jira**.
import.jiraApiWhat1: Issues (Stories, Tasks, Bugs) → Tasks (with priority and status)
import.jiraApiWhat3: Epics → Epics (Atlassian Document Format descriptions are converted to plain text)
import.postImportDesc: Data lands in Kanban — here is what to do next
import.postImportBody: All imported data starts in a new Kanban project. Take these steps to get your team productive immediately:
import.postImportItem1Desc: Open the new project's backlog and scan for any tasks that need re-assignment or status corrections.
import.postImportItem2Desc: Go to Project Settings → Members and add your teammates to the project.
import.postImportItem3Desc: In Project Settings, switch from Kanban to Scrum (for sprint-based work) or Shape Up (for 6-week cycles) when your team is ready.
import.errorRecoveryDesc: What to do if your import partially fails or does not start
import.errorRowsDesc: Individual row failures do not block the rest of the import. The results screen shows a per-row error log.
import.errorRowsStep1: Download the error report from the Import History page.
import.errorRowsStep2: Fix the highlighted columns in your CSV file (refer to the error message for each row).
import.errorRowsStep3: Re-upload only the corrected rows as a new import (the project already exists — tasks will be added to it).
import.errorApiDesc: If the OAuth popup closes without completing or the import times out:
import.errorApiItem1: Check that your browser is not blocking the popup.
import.errorApiItem2: Ensure you authorized the correct account (Atlassian or Linear workspace).
import.errorApiItem3: Try disconnecting and reconnecting the integration from Organization Settings.
import.errorTipDesc: Import History (accessible from the Import page) keeps a record of every past import with its status and row counts. Use it to track re-import attempts.

scrumMode.title: Scrum Mode
scrumMode.subtitle: Run time-boxed sprints, track story points, and measure velocity using ShipFlow's Scrum project type.
scrumMode.scrumOnlyNoticeDesc: This guide applies to projects created with the Scrum project type. Kanban projects use continuous flow and Shape Up projects use 6-week cycles. See the
scrumMode.whatDesc: Scrum mode adapts ShipFlow's cycle infrastructure into time-boxed sprints with sprint goals, story-point estimation, burndown charts, and velocity tracking. It is the third project type alongside Shape Up and Kanban.
scrumMode.conceptSprintsDesc: Fixed-length work periods (1–4 weeks). Each sprint has a goal, a start date, and an end date. Cycles in ShipFlow become sprints in Scrum mode.
scrumMode.conceptVelocityDesc: The average story points completed per sprint, calculated automatically from historical sprint data. Use it to forecast how much work fits in the next sprint.
scrumMode.conceptBacklogDesc: The prioritized list of all work items waiting to be assigned to a sprint. Teams refine and re-order this continuously.
scrumMode.conceptStoryPointsDesc: A relative unit of effort assigned to each task. Points roll up to sprint totals and power burndown and velocity charts.
scrumMode.whatNoteDesc: Shape Up uses 6-week fixed cycles where scope is flexible. Scrum uses shorter sprints with a sprint goal and a committed backlog. Both are fully supported in ShipFlow.
scrumMode.step1Item1: Go to **Projects** in the sidebar and click **New Project**.
scrumMode.step1Item2: Enter the project name and description.
scrumMode.step1Item3: In the **Project Type** dropdown, select **Scrum**. You will also set:
scrumMode.step1Item4: Click **Create Project**. ShipFlow creates the project with an empty backlog ready for sprint planning.
scrumMode.step1TipDesc: You can choose Scrum as the target project type during import. All sprints and issues will be mapped automatically.
scrumMode.step2Subtitle: Create a sprint, set the goal, and fill the sprint backlog
scrumMode.step2Desc: Sprint planning is done from the dedicated Sprint Planning page, accessible via the Cycles menu.
scrumMode.step2Item2: Set the sprint **name**, **start date**, **end date**, and **sprint goal**.
scrumMode.step2Item3: In the **Sprint Planning** view, the left column shows the product backlog and the right shows the new sprint.
scrumMode.step2Item4: Drag tasks from the backlog into the sprint, or click the **→** arrow to move them. Story point totals update live.
scrumMode.step2Item5: Click **Start Sprint** when the team is ready to begin.
scrumMode.step2TipDesc: The sprint total story points are shown at the top of the sprint column. Compare against your team's historical velocity to avoid over-committing.
scrumMode.step3Subtitle: Track progress through story points and the sprint board
scrumMode.step3Desc: During the sprint, the team moves tasks across the sprint board and updates story-point completion as work progresses.
scrumMode.step3StoryPointsDesc: Open any task to set or update its story point estimate. Story points on the task feed into the burndown chart automatically — no manual entry required.
scrumMode.step3BoardDesc: The sprint board shows tasks in Kanban-style columns. Move tasks between columns to track progress:
scrumMode.step3BoardItem1: To Do — tasks not yet started
scrumMode.step3BoardItem2: In Progress — work actively being done
scrumMode.step3BoardItem3: Done — completed tasks; story points are automatically burned down
scrumMode.step3BurndownDesc: The real-time burndown chart compares remaining story points against the ideal trajectory. Navigate to the sprint detail page to see it. Deviations above the ideal line signal scope creep or a progress lull.
scrumMode.step3WarnItem1: Burndown is flat or rising — stop adding work and identify blockers
scrumMode.step3WarnItem2: Story points are not being estimated — the burndown will be inaccurate; run an estimation session
scrumMode.step4Subtitle: Review outcomes and learn from the data
scrumMode.step4Desc: At the end of the sprint, hold a sprint review meeting to demo completed work, then close the sprint in ShipFlow to freeze the velocity data.
scrumMode.step4VelocityDesc: The velocity chart shows planned vs completed story points across past sprints. Access it from the project's Reports tab.
scrumMode.step4VelocityStep1: Go to the project and click **Reports**.
scrumMode.step4VelocityStep3: Use the historical average to decide how many story points to commit in the next sprint.
scrumMode.step4RetroDesc: After the review, run a retrospective using ShipFlow's Retrospectives feature. Document what went well, what to improve, and action items for the next sprint.
scrumMode.bp1Desc: Start with 2-week sprints. Shorter sprints surface problems faster and allow the team to adapt more frequently.
scrumMode.bp2Desc: Hold a backlog refinement session before sprint planning so story points are already on tasks. Planning goes faster when items are pre-estimated.
scrumMode.bp3Desc: Avoid adding new work mid-sprint. If urgent work must be added, explicitly remove something of equivalent size.
scrumMode.bp4Desc: Always close the sprint on its end date even if some tasks are not done. Move incomplete tasks to the backlog and start fresh.

migration.title: Migrating to ShipFlow
migration.subtitle: A step-by-step guide for moving your team from Jira, Linear, or Asana to ShipFlow.
migration.whyDesc: A brief look at what you gain by switching
migration.whyBody: ShipFlow is a methodology-first project management platform built for teams that want to work intentionally — whether through Shape Up cycles, Scrum sprints, or Kanban flow. Key advantages over traditional tools:
migration.whyItem1: First-class Shape Up support — pitches, betting table, hill charts, and cool-down periods built-in.
migration.whyItem2: Open source and self-hostable — no per-seat pricing; run it on your own infrastructure.
migration.whyItem3: AI features (Risk Advisor, Wise Architecture, QA Test Generation) included, not add-ons.
migration.whyItem4: All three methodologies (Shape Up, Scrum, Kanban) in a single platform — switch per project.
migration.jiraDesc: Two options: CSV export or direct Jira API import
migration.jiraCsvStep1: In Jira, go to **Project settings** → **Export issues**.
migration.jiraCsvStep2: Choose **Export Excel CSV (all fields)** and save the file.
migration.jiraCsvStep3: In ShipFlow, go to **Import** → **CSV** tab, drag-and-drop the file, and confirm.
migration.jiraCsvStep4: ShipFlow auto-detects the Jira format and maps issues, epics, and sprints.
migration.jiraApiStep1: In ShipFlow, go to **Import** → **Jira** tab and click **Connect Jira**.
migration.jiraApiStep2: Complete the Atlassian OAuth 2.0 authorization in the popup window.
migration.jiraApiStep3: Select your Jira project, choose a target project type (Kanban or Scrum), and click **Import from Jira**.
migration.jiraGotcha1: Custom fields are not imported — only standard fields (summary, description, status, priority, assignee).
migration.jiraGotcha2: File attachments are not transferred — download attachments manually and re-upload them in ShipFlow.
migration.jiraGotcha3: Jira subtasks are imported as top-level tasks, not nested under a parent.
migration.linearDesc: Use the OAuth2-powered Linear API import for the smoothest experience
migration.linearBody: Linear and ShipFlow share a similar model — both center on cycles and issues. The API import preserves priority, state, and assignee for all issues.
migration.linearStep1: In ShipFlow, go to **Import** → **Linear** tab and click **Connect Linear**.
migration.linearStep2: Authorize ShipFlow in the Linear OAuth2 popup.
migration.linearStep3: Select your Linear team from the dropdown.
migration.linearStep4: Enter a project name, choose Kanban or Scrum, and click **Import from Linear**.
migration.linearNote: Linear CSV import is also supported.
migration.linearNoteDesc: Go to Linear Settings → Export data → Issues CSV if you prefer a file-based migration.
migration.asanaDesc: CSV-only import — direct API import for Asana is planned for a future release
migration.asanaBody: Asana API import is on the roadmap. For now, use the CSV export path.
migration.asanaStep1: In Asana, open your project, click the **three-dot menu**, and select **Export / Print** → **CSV**.
migration.asanaStep2: Asana will email you the CSV file. Download it.
migration.asanaStep3: In ShipFlow, go to **Import** → **CSV** tab and upload the file. ShipFlow detects the Asana format automatically.
migration.asanaStep4: Review the preview and confirm the import.
migration.asanaNoteDesc: Custom fields, subtasks, and file attachments are not imported via CSV. Sections map to Kanban statuses.
migration.afterDesc: Set up your team and choose your methodology
migration.afterBody: Once the import completes, your data is in a Kanban project. Follow these steps to complete the onboarding:
migration.afterTeamStep1: Go to the new project and open **Project Settings → Members**.
migration.afterTeamStep2: Invite team members by email. They will receive a ShipFlow invitation.
migration.afterTeamStep3: Assign roles (Developer, QA, Product, Viewer) to match your team structure.
migration.afterMethodologyDesc: All imports default to Kanban. Switch from Project Settings when your team is ready:
migration.afterMethodologyKanban: Keep continuous flow with swimlane columns. Good for support and ops teams.
migration.afterMethodologyScrum: Switch to sprint-based delivery. Requires story-point estimates on tasks.
migration.afterMethodologyShapeUp: Switch to 6-week cycles with pitches and betting. Best for product teams shipping features.
migration.afterNote: Take it one step at a time.
migration.afterNoteDesc: Start with Kanban to get the team familiar with ShipFlow, then migrate to Scrum or Shape Up once everyone is comfortable.

mcpIntegration.serverConfigurationDescription: MCP servers must be configured by your system administrator using environment variables. Contact your admin to enable MCP integration:
mcpIntegration.tokensDescription: Access tokens are stored securely per-organization and are used to authenticate with GitHub and Figma APIs. Tokens are never displayed after being saved.
mcpIntegration.serverDescription: Let AI tools like Claude Code connect directly to ShipFlow over MCP.
mcpIntegration.serverEnableHint: Allow external AI tools to query and act on ShipFlow data.
mcpIntegration.serverWriteHint: Allow connected tools to create and update data, not just read it.
mcpIntegration.serverToggleError: Failed to update MCP server settings.
mcpIntegration.connectIntro: Point your MCP client at the SSE endpoint below and authenticate with an API key.
mcpIntegration.connectKeyHint: Create an API key in the API Keys tab and use it as the bearer token.

mcpIntegration.connectorUrlAltHint: For hosted clients like claude.ai connectors that can't set custom HTTP headers, paste a single URL with the API key embedded in the path instead:

Because the key sits in the URL, it can be logged by proxies and browser history, so use a dedicated, short-lived, easily-rotated key scoped to only what you want this connector to do.

mcpIntegration.sharepointSiteUrlHint: Format: hostname:/sites/path — e.g. contoso.sharepoint.com:/sites/Engineering. Or paste the site GUID directly.

inboundWebhooks.subtitle: Configure external services to send events to ShipFlow
inboundWebhooks.howItWorksDesc: External services send signed HTTP POST requests to ShipFlow. Configure a provider's name, webhook URL, HMAC secret, and signature header without writing any code.

webhooksGuide.outgoingDesc: Send events from ShipFlow to external services like Slack and Microsoft Teams
webhooksGuide.outgoingIntro: ShipFlow can send notifications to Slack and MS Teams when important events occur in your cycles and pitches.
webhooksGuide.slackStep1: Go to Organization Settings → Integrations → Slack
webhooksGuide.slackStep2: Generate an Incoming Webhook URL from your Slack workspace
webhooksGuide.slackStep3: Paste the URL and configure which events trigger notifications
webhooksGuide.stagnationDesc: Automatic notifications are sent when a scope has not progressed past the peak of the hill chart for an extended period.
webhooksGuide.inboundDesc: Receive events from external services and trigger actions in ShipFlow
webhooksGuide.inboundIntro: Inbound webhooks allow external services like Zendesk, PagerDuty, or custom systems to push events into ShipFlow securely.
webhooksGuide.howToConnect: How to Connect an External Service
webhooksGuide.step1Desc: Go to Integrations → Inbound Webhooks and click Add Provider
webhooksGuide.step2Desc: Copy the webhook URL and paste it into your external service, along with the shared secret
webhooksGuide.step3a: ShipFlow verifies each request using HMAC signature validation
webhooksGuide.step3c: The signature header name must match what the external service sends
webhooksGuide.step3d: Requests with invalid signatures are rejected with a 401 error
webhooksGuide.step4Desc: Send a test event from the external service and check ShipFlow logs
webhooksGuide.securityDesc: All inbound webhook requests are verified using HMAC signatures. Each provider has its own unique secret, and the signature is checked before any event is processed.
webhooksGuide.listProvidersDesc: GET /api/webhooks/providers — Returns all configured webhook providers for your organization
webhooksGuide.eventHeadersDesc: Each inbound request includes provider metadata headers for routing and auditing
webhooksGuide.providersDesc: ShipFlow supports any HTTP-based webhook provider that can send HMAC-signed requests
